meta.name: Flame in Freefall seed dataset
meta.generation_note: SI-assisted: compiled with the help of an AI assistant from public NASA fact sheets and the Space Apps challenge brief, then reviewed by the team. Values are only filled where a source states them; null means not stated in our sources, not zero.

habitats.name: Moon base
habitats.note: Brief: likely 30% O2 or more at 10.2 psi or less, over 40% more oxygen than Earth air, so materials are much more flammable.

habitats.name: Pressurised rover
habitats.note: Brief groups rovers with the Moon base atmosphere.

habitats.name: Mars base
habitats.note: ASSUMPTION: no Mars atmosphere is given in our sources; we assume a Moon-base-like atmosphere. State this in the pitch.

investigations.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids
investigations.o2_note: O2 not stated in our sources. BASS (2012) ran before N2 dilution was introduced (first used in BASS-II, NTRS 20210011385), so likely cabin air, but no value found. Pressure 1 atm from the BASS and BASS-II fabric paper (NTRS 20150008962).
investigations.flow_note: Kept 5-50 cm/s (matches the spaceflight101 BASS-II description). Sources differ: PSI-26 says airflow up to 40 cm/s, and a NASA BASS-II presentation (NTRS 20160000593) lists 0-55 cm/s as the main variable range. Recheck against the bass_sheet wording.
investigations.geometry: Thin flat 12 x 1-2 cm; thick flat 5 x 1 cm x 1-2 mm; PMMA spheres 1-2 cm; candles 6 x 25 mm
investigations.variables: Material, thickness, shape, airflow speed, N2 suppressant flow
key_findings: Tests whether materials burn as well or better in microgravity when ventilation is adequate.
Best place to apply suppressant is harder to find in microgravity; badly placed suppressant can feed the flame by pulling in oxygen.
investigations.people: PI Paul Ferkul (NCSER); Sandra Olson (NASA GRC)

investigations.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids II
investigations.o2_note: PSI-25 BASS-II table, Calibrated initial O2 column: 13.6 to 22.2% across the tests (read from a screenshot, so allow +/-0.1). NASA papers (NTRS 20150008962, 20160000593) quote 16-21% for the fabric tests. Pressure 1 atm from NTRS 20150008962 (PSI-25 has no pressure column).
investigations.flow_note: PSI-25 'Air display' column: readings from 0 up to 49 (units not labelled, read as cm/s). PSI-26 description says airflow up to 40 cm/s and a NASA presentation (NTRS 20160000593) lists 0-55 cm/s. Recheck against the bass_sheet.
investigations.geometry: Thin flat 10 x 1-2 cm; rods; large sphere section
investigations.variables: Ambient O2, airflow speed, fuel type and thickness, opposed vs concurrent flow
key_findings: Measured minimum O2 and flow needed for materials to burn in space and compared with Earth upward-burning limits.
Thin and thick fuel spread rates measured, plus a formula for the thin-to-thick transition.
Models predicted faster flame spread than observed, so models need improvement.
Data supports theoretical quenching boundaries.

investigations.name: BASS-Milliken (flame-retardant textiles)
investigations.o2_note: No BASS-M O2 or pressure values found yet. Uses the same MSG + SPICE hardware as BASS. Check the BASS-M PSI page.
investigations.flow_note: Same 5-50 cm/s as the BASS entries; not checked separately for BASS-M.
investigations.geometry: 44 textile samples with integrated igniter wires
key_findings: Compares microgravity behaviour of flame-retardant fabrics with Earth behaviour; NASA screening uses upward-burning tests that ignore microgravity.

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration I
investigations.o2_note: PSI Saffire-I sample table: S1 21.5-21.7% O2, S2 ~21.5% O2. Pressure 100 kPa (0.99 atm) from Urban et al., ICES-2021-266, Table 2 (not in the PSI table).
investigations.flow_note: PSI Saffire-I sample table: 20 cm/s for both samples (S1 concurrent, S2 opposed).
investigations.hardware: Cygnus cargo vehicle after leaving ISS
key_findings: First large-scale fire in space; the previous largest space fire test was about index-card sized.

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration II
investigations.o2_note: PSI Saffire-II table, samples 2-1 to 2-5 only (5 of 16 rows seen): ~21.5 to ~22.1% O2. Pressure 100 kPa (0.99 atm) from Urban et al., ICES-2021-266, Table 2. Other 11 samples not yet checked.
investigations.flow_note: PSI Saffire-II samples 2-1 to 2-5: 20 cm/s. Upper value 25 cm/s from Urban et al., ICES-2021-266, Table 2 (sample II-6).
investigations.hardware: Cygnus cargo vehicle after leaving ISS
key_findings: Widened the range of spacecraft materials burned at large scale.

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration III
investigations.o2_note: O2 and pressure not in the PSI Saffire-III table. 21% O2 and 100 kPa (0.99 atm) from Urban et al., ICES-2021-266, Table 2 (sample III-1).
investigations.flow_note: Higher flow velocity than Saffire-I. PSI Saffire-III table: 30 cm/s for both samples (S1 concurrent, S2 opposed). ICES-2021-266 Table 2 lists 25 cm/s for III-1. The two sources disagree, so both are kept as the range.
investigations.hardware: Cygnus cargo vehicle after leaving ISS
key_findings: Repeated Saffire-I material at a higher airflow to see how ventilation changes large-scale fire growth.

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration IV to VI
investigations.o2_note: Varied pressure and O2 toward exploration-vehicle atmospheres; values not stated. Not named in the challenge brief, check PSI for data. Values from Urban et al.: ICES-2021-266 Table 1 (Saffire IV 22.0% O2 and 100 kPa, Saffire V 25.4-26.2% O2 and 70.7-72.6 kPa) and ICES-2024-365 Table 1 (Saffire VI 28.8-31.0% O2 and 54.1-55.2 kPa). Pressure converted to atm (54.1 kPa = 0.53). Saffire VI covers only the three tests reported in that paper.
investigations.flow_note: Same two papers: 20 cm/s, reduced to 5 cm/s in some tests (IV-2, V-3, V-4, VI-3).
investigations.hardware: Cygnus cargo vehicle after leaving ISS
measurements: VI: fire detection, combustion product monitoring, post-fire cleanup
key_findings: Glowing char seen behind the flame front (IV).
V and VI target exploration spacecraft pressure and O2 ranges.

investigations.name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment
investigations.variables: Airflow rate, heating temperature, smoke aging time
key_findings: Much of the smoke mass is in particles larger than 1 micron; Teflon smoke is mostly under 1 micron.
Mean particle diameters were 100 to 200 nm.
Aging cuts particle count a lot while mass stays steady (coagulation).
Detectors need to cover a wide size range; early detection should target pyrolysis products, not soot.
investigations.people: PI David Urban (NASA GRC); NIST collaborators

investigations.name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Reflight
measurements: commercial, ISS and Shuttle smoke detectors
key_findings: Compared flight and ground results and tested the real ISS and Shuttle detectors.
Shuttle detectors were ionization-based; ISS detectors use near-IR scattering and are most sensitive above 1 micron, so each misses part of the size range.

investigations.name: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT and DAFT-2)
key_findings: Confirmed the modified P-Trak works in microgravity before it was used for smoke in SAME.
Useful for telling dust from smoke, which matters for false alarms (lunar dust).

investigations.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.variables: O2 level, suppressant type and amount, pressure, fuel, droplet size
key_findings: Measured how well CO2 and He suppress flames in microgravity and estimated the limiting oxygen index.
Low-pressure suppression data supports strategies like isolating a module and venting the cabin.
Cool flames were first seen in ISS droplet tests in 2012 (per ACME sheet).

investigations.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment 2
investigations.flow_note: Sub-buoyant convective flow by moving a tethered droplet; speed not stated.
investigations.geometry: Droplets 2-4 mm; tethered moving droplets; 2-droplet arrays
investigations.variables: Fuel mixture, convective flow, droplet spacing
key_findings: Extends droplet burning to practical fuels, moving droplets and droplet-to-droplet flame spread.
investigations.people: Lead PI Forman Williams (UCSD); JAXA and ASI partners

investigations.name: Cool Flames Investigation
investigations.todo: Fill from PSI page: fuels, O2, pressure.
key_findings: Follows up the 2012 ISS discovery of cool flames around droplets, which burn at low temperature and are hard to see.

investigations.name: ACME Burning Rate Emulator
fuels: gaseous fuels emulating paper, plastic and alcohol
investigations.geometry: Flat porous burner with heat flux sensors and surface thermocouple
key_findings: Only ACME experiment aimed at fire prevention; tests material flammability in still air and checks flammability test methods for low and partial gravity.

investigations.name: ACME Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
investigations.o2_note: Highest O2 in PSI microgravity tests: O2/N2 up to 85% O2 flowed from the burner into a fuel/N2 chamber (brief).
fuels: propane and other gases in the chamber
key_findings: Only microgravity data at very high oxygen, so the closest match for oxygen-rich habitats and suits.

investigations.name: ACME Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
key_findings: Sooty microgravity flames are taller, wider and cooler, with 5 to 8 times more soot than on Earth.
Diluted microgravity flames are more stable and lift off at lower fuel levels.

investigations.name: ACME Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
investigations.geometry: Insulated burner with mesh electrode 35-50 mm away, up to 10 kV
key_findings: Electric field acts on flame ions to mimic partial gravity, the only PSI proxy for Moon/Mars gravity.

investigations.name: ACME Flame Design
key_findings: Flammability and soot limits under oxygen enrichment.

investigations.name: ACME Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
key_findings: Extinction behaviour of sooty and soot-free flames in still air.

investigations.name: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.geometry: Small gas jets (lighter-sized), several nozzle diameters
key_findings: Soot controls radiant heat from fires, so smoke point data improves heat release predictions for spacecraft fires.
Could support performance-based material selection.
investigations.people: PI David Urban (NASA GRC); Peter Sunderland (UMD)

investigations.name: Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
investigations.variables: Fuel, dilution, nozzle diameter, coflow speed
key_findings: Flame attachment and liftoff limits as air speed rises; precursor to ACME CLD.

future.name: Flammability of Materials on the Moon
future.note: First combustion experiment on another planetary body. Partial gravity data not yet in PSI.

future.name: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction
future.note: ISS fire growth study; notes NASA-STD-6001 may not be conservative in low gravity.

future.name: Flammability Limits At Reduced-g Experiment
future.note: Relates Earth and microgravity flammability limits so space limits can be estimated from ground tests.

incidents.name: Apollo 1
incidents.summary: Flash fire in the Command Module during a pad test killed the three crew. 100% oxygen cabin, likely wire arcing, combustible materials, hatch could not open against pressure.
incidents.lessons: Restrict combustible materials, fire-resistant suits, quick-opening hatch, hazard reviews for all tests.

incidents.name: Apollo 13
incidents.summary: Oxygen tank exploded on day 3 after heaters overheated during a pad test and damaged Teflon wire insulation. Crew used the Lunar Module as a lifeboat.
incidents.lessons: Redesigned oxygen storage, upgraded thermostats, sheathed wiring.

incidents.name: Mir fire
incidents.summary: Solid-fuel oxygen generator canister caught fire, filled the module with smoke and blocked a Soyuz escape vehicle. Burned several minutes; smoke took hours to clear.
incidents.lessons: Better emergency training, canister preparation, redundant oxygen systems on ISS.

incidents.name: Artemis II smoke alarm
incidents.summary: Smoke alarm went off during the crewed lunar flyby mission, about 80,000 miles from Earth (brief).
incidents.lessons: Detection reliability and false alarms matter far from home.

spinoffs.name: Firefighter air tanks
spinoffs.summary: Lighter composite air tanks from spacesuit work: 30 min air at about 13 lb lighter.

spinoffs.name: Smoke vs dust fire detector
spinoffs.summary: Shuttle-derived detector that ignores dust, so fewer false alarms; used in mines.

spinoffs.name: Firefighter protective clothing
spinoffs.summary: Spacesuit fire-resistant materials applied to firefighter gear (Project FIRES).

spinoffs.name: Fine water mist extinguishers
spinoffs.summary: Developed for ISS, now used on Earth (brief).
